articles.body: Day 1 of a new series on Microsoft 365 licensing and customization, checked against Microsoft's own plan comparison and service descriptions (October 2026). This week a colourful "Microsoft 365 Enterprise Licenses" chart landed in my feed. Nice icons, green ticks, red crosses, a little handwritten "A more productive and secure tomorrow". Very shareable. Also wrong in about ten places, and some of those mistakes cost real money: buy F3 because the chart says it has Defender for Office 365, and your frontline staff get phishing protection that is a lot thinner than you think. So I rebuilt the chart from Microsoft's documents, and then did the part no chart can do: checked what a tenant actually owns, and turned off one service inside a license without touching the rest.

articles.title: A Free Random Color Generator I Built for Designers and Developers
articles.excerpt: Colors are one of those things that seem simple until you need one. "Just pick a nice blue" sounds easy, and then you spend forty minutes cycling through a color picker, squinting at slightly differen…
articles.body: Colors are one of those things that seem simple until you need one. "Just pick a nice blue" sounds easy, and then you spend forty minutes cycling through a color picker, squinting at slightly different shades of the same blue, and going in circles. I have lost more hours to this than I care to admit, which is why I eventually built myself a random color generator and put it on my site for anyone to use. This post is about what the tool does, how I built it, and the real use cases where a random color button beats a color picker. What the tool does The idea is deliberately simple. You open the page, you click generate, and you get a random color with its HEX, RGB, and HSL values.

articles.title: How to Run a Fair Secret Santa Draw Online (Free, No Signup)
articles.excerpt: Every December the same scene plays out in offices and group chats: someone volunteers to organize Secret Santa, everyone is excited, and then the organizer realizes they are stuck doing the draw. Nam…
articles.body: Every December the same scene plays out in offices and group chats: someone volunteers to organize Secret Santa, everyone is excited, and then the organizer realizes they are stuck doing the draw. Names in a hat work when everyone is in one room. For a remote team or a group of friends spread across cities, the hat trick falls apart. And there is always the awkward moment when someone draws their own name, or a couple draws each other and everyone groans. I ran into this exact problem a couple of years ago. I was organizing a Secret Santa for a group of old friends, and I kept messing up the draw because of the couple problem: we had two couples in the group, and every exclusion rule made the paper-slip method miserable.

articles.title: How to Check HTTP Status Codes in Bulk with PHP and curl_multi
articles.excerpt: Checking a single URL's HTTP status is trivial. One curl request, done. But when you need to check 50, 100, or 500 URLs at once — for example, when auditing a client's site for broken links — the naiv…
articles.body: Checking a single URL's HTTP status is trivial. One curl request, done. But when you need to check 50, 100, or 500 URLs at once — for example, when auditing a client's site for broken links — the naive approach falls apart fast. I ran into this while building Site Tools Box , a free toolbox for webmasters. The bulk HTTP checker was one of the first tools I built, and I got the concurrency wrong three times before landing on the right pattern. Here's what actually works. Why Sequential Requests Are Too Slow The obvious approach: loop through URLs, call curl_exec on each, collect results.

articles.title: Architecting a Low-Power GPS Geofencing Engine for Android without Draining the Battery
articles.excerpt: It was the middle of a Friday afternoon prayer session. The mosque was silent, save for the rhythmic recitation of the Imam. Suddenly, a sharp, upbeat ringtone cut through the quiet like a knife. The…
articles.body: It was the middle of a Friday afternoon prayer session. The mosque was silent, save for the rhythmic recitation of the Imam. Suddenly, a sharp, upbeat ringtone cut through the quiet like a knife. The person next to me fumbled, panicked, and eventually silenced their device, but the damage was done. The embarrassment on their face was palpable. We have all been there. Whether it is a boardroom meeting, a final exam, or a quiet moment of reflection, the social cost of a forgotten ringer is high. I sat there thinking, why is this still a manual process in 2026? My phone knows where I am. It knows the current time. It knows my calendar. Yet, it sits there, passive and waiting for me to remember to flip a physical switch.

articles.excerpt: Apple has finally announced its long-rumored foldable: the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display, a “nano‑texture” finish on the inner screen, and barely…
articles.body: Apple has finally announced its long-rumored foldable: the iPhone Duo . The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display, a “nano‑texture” finish on the inner screen, and barely any visible crease. Instead of Face ID, it uses Touch ID on the power button. It has two cameras, a main lens and a wide-angle lens. Apple completely revamped iOS 27’s controls and apps for the foldable, including putting the dock on the side of the phone. And it has a flashy opening animation when you unfold the phone. The iPhone Duo a big new bet from Apple, though one that’s a little late to the game compared to competitors like Samsung and Google. The phone isn’t cheap: it starts at $1,999 for the base 256GB model, and the prices only go up from there.

articles.excerpt: The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission wish that we could all see Earth as they just did —as a beautiful but fragile outpost of life in a vast void.
articles.body: The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did. An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA. "You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere , and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission .

articles.body: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside.

articles.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
articles.excerpt: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have unravelled some of the secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot exoplanet that has the consistency of marshmallow.
articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
articles.excerpt: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show? articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES weather satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space.
